items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Millennium Development Goals (MDGs)"?
options: Economic growth that is decoupled from environmental damage through clean technology, efficiency and markets
The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, adopted at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit, which provides the framework for climate negotiations
Nine environmental limits within which humanity can safely operate, identified by Johan Rockström and colleagues in 2009
Eight international development goals for 2000–2015, including halving extreme poverty and achieving universal primary education
items.answer: Eight international development goals for 2000–2015, including halving extreme poverty and achieving universal primary education
items.markingKey: D. "Millennium Development Goals (MDGs)" is eight international development goals for 2000–2015, including halving extreme poverty and achieving universal primary education.

items.stem: A student claims that the SDGs are a legally binding treaty with sanctions for non-compliance. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The SDGs are a political commitment adopted by the General Assembly; progress is reviewed voluntarily (Voluntary National Reviews at the High-Level Political Forum) without sanctions.
items.markingKey: The SDGs are a political commitment adopted by the General Assembly; progress is reviewed voluntarily (Voluntary National Reviews at the High-Level Political Forum) without sanctions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that sustainable development means stopping economic growth. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The Brundtland concept seeks to balance growth with social and environmental goals; debates exist over whether growth can be made green, but sustainable development does not by definition require zero growth.
items.markingKey: The Brundtland concept seeks to balance growth with social and environmental goals; debates exist over whether growth can be made green, but sustainable development does not by definition require zero growth. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Identify which SDG is most directly addressed by each: (a) a programme to provide free school meals, (b) a new solar farm, (c) a law to protect mangrove forests.
items.answer: (a) SDG 2 Zero Hunger (also SDG 4 Quality Education); (b) SDG 7 Affordable and Clean Energy (also SDG 13); (c) SDG 14 Life Below Water / SDG 15 Life on Land / SDG 13. 1 mark each.
items.markingKey: (a) SDG 2 Zero Hunger (also SDG 4 Quality Education); (b) SDG 7 Affordable and Clean Energy (also SDG 13); (c) SDG 14 Life Below Water / SDG 15 Life on Land / SDG 13. 1 mark each.

items.stem: Using SDG 6 and water in Cape Town as an example, explain the environmental pillar of sustainability.
items.answer: In 2018 Cape Town nearly reached "Day Zero" when taps would be shut off; strict rationing reduced consumption by about half. a climate-linked drought showed how environmental stress threatens development and requires collective action
items.markingKey: Context (In 2018 Cape Town nearly reached "Day Zero" when taps would be shut off; strict rationing reduced consumption by about half.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: a climate-linked drought showed how environmental stress threatens development and requires collective action – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the environmental pillar of sustainability.

items.stem: Outline one way in which MDG 1 on extreme poverty shows the achievements and limits of global goals.
items.answer: The target of halving the proportion of people in extreme poverty between 1990 and 2015 was met early, largely due to growth in China and India. global targets coincided with major progress, but much was driven by national growth rather than the goals themselves
items.markingKey: Context (The target of halving the proportion of people in extreme poverty between 1990 and 2015 was met early, largely due to growth in China and India.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: global targets coincided with major progress, but much was driven by national growth rather than the goals themselves – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the achievements and limits of global goals.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that sustainable development is a contradiction in terms.
items.answer: There is real tension, but sustainable development is possible if growth is decoupled from environmental harm – something only partly achieved so far.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: growth increases resource use; Limits to Growth; degrowth critiques. Arguments against: decoupling in some countries; renewable energy growth; Costa Rica, Denmark. Supported judgement: There is real tension, but sustainable development is possible if growth is decoupled from environmental harm – something only partly achieved so far.

items.stem: Evaluate the progress of one country you have studied towards the Sustainable Development Goals.
items.answer: Choose a country and 2–3 SDGs; use data (VNRs, SDG Index), identify successes and failures and explain them (governance, finance, conflict, climate).
items.markingKey: Choose a country and 2–3 SDGs; use data (VNRs, SDG Index), identify successes and failures and explain them (governance, finance, conflict, climate).

items.stem: Explain why progress towards the SDGs has slowed since 2020.
items.answer: COVID-19, conflicts (Ukraine, Sudan), inflation, debt crises and climate disasters reversed gains; the UN reported in 2024 that only about 17% of targets were on track.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: COVID-19, conflicts (Ukraine, Sudan), inflation, debt crises and climate disasters reversed gains; the UN reported in 2024 that only about 17% of targets were on track. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why the SDGs are considered more comprehensive than the MDGs.
items.answer: The SDGs cover economic, social and environmental goals (including climate, oceans, inequality, peace and institutions), apply to all countries, and were negotiated with wider participation, whereas the MDGs focused mainly on poverty, health and education in developing countries.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The SDGs cover economic, social and environmental goals (including climate, oceans, inequality, peace and institutions), apply to all countries, and were negotiated with wider participation, whereas the MDGs focused mainly on poverty, health and education in developing countries. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Alessia writes: "The SDGs are a legally binding treaty with sanctions for non-compliance." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The SDGs are a political commitment adopted by the General Assembly; progress is reviewed voluntarily (Voluntary National Reviews at the High-Level Political Forum) without sanctions.
items.markingKey: The SDGs are a political commitment adopted by the General Assembly; progress is reviewed voluntarily (Voluntary National Reviews at the High-Level Political Forum) without sanctions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Halfway to 2030, the promise of the SDGs is in peril. Too many targets are off track, and some have gone into reverse."
— Paraphrase of UN Secretary-General António Guterres, SDG progress report, 2023

Explain, with reference to the source, two reasons why the SDGs may be off track.
items.answer: Shocks such as COVID-19, conflicts, debt crises and climate disasters reversed progress; insufficient financing and political will mean targets are not met.
items.markingKey: Shocks such as COVID-19, conflicts, debt crises and climate disasters reversed progress; insufficient financing and political will mean targets are not met. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: "The Sustainable Development Goals are too ambitious to be achieved." Discuss.
items.answer: Most SDGs will not be met by 2030, but their value lies in shaping priorities and accountability rather than full achievement.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: 17 goals and 169 targets; only a small share on track; financing gap of trillions. Arguments against: goals set direction and mobilise action; MDGs saw real progress; universal framework. Supported judgement: Most SDGs will not be met by 2030, but their value lies in shaping priorities and accountability rather than full achievement. items.answer: There is real tension, but sustainable development is possible if growth is decoupled from environmental harm – something only partly achieved so far.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: growth increases resource use; Limits to Growth; degrowth critiques. Arguments against: decoupling in some countries; renewable energy growth; Costa Rica, Denmark. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The 2015 agreement in which all parties pledged nationally determined contributions to hold warming well below 2°C and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C"?
items.answer: Paris Agreement
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of Paris Agreement.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement.
items.answer: Kyoto set top-down legally binding emission targets for developed countries only; Paris uses bottom-up, self-determined pledges (NDCs) from all parties, with binding procedural obligations to report and update but not to achieve targets.
items.markingKey: Kyoto set top-down legally binding emission targets for developed countries only; Paris uses bottom-up, self-determined pledges (NDCs) from all parties, with binding procedural obligations to report and update but not to achieve targets. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why the Paris Agreement is criticised for being weak.
items.answer: NDCs are voluntary and not legally enforceable; current pledges put the world on course for around 2.5–3°C of warming, and states can withdraw (the US did in 2020 and again in 2025). (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: NDCs are voluntary and not legally enforceable; current pledges put the world on course for around 2.5–3°C of warming, and states can withdraw (the US did in 2020 and again in 2025). (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe the ICJ advisory opinion on climate change (2025) and explain what it reveals about legal approaches to climate justice.
items.answer: Following a campaign started by Pacific law students and a General Assembly request led by Vanuatu, the ICJ advised in July 2025 that states have legal obligations to prevent significant climate harm. small states used international law to strengthen claims on major emitters
items.markingKey: Context (Following a campaign started by Pacific law students and a General Assembly request led by Vanuatu, the ICJ advised in July 2025 that states have legal obligations to prevent significant climate harm.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: small states used international law to strengthen claims on major emitters – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to legal approaches to climate justice.

items.stem: Classify each as mitigation or adaptation: (a) Bangladesh building cyclone shelters, (b) the EU Emissions Trading System, (c) the Netherlands raising dykes, (d) Kenya expanding geothermal power.
items.answer: (a) adaptation; (b) mitigation; (c) adaptation; (d) mitigation. 1 mark each.
items.markingKey: (a) adaptation; (b) mitigation; (c) adaptation; (d) mitigation. 1 mark each.

items.stem: Analyse why international cooperation on climate change has been difficult, using one theoretical perspective.
items.answer: E.g. realism (relative gains, national interest), liberal institutionalism (Paris as regime), Marxism/dependency (North–South inequality). Use COP examples and evaluate the perspective.
items.markingKey: E.g. realism (relative gains, national interest), liberal institutionalism (Paris as regime), Marxism/dependency (North–South inequality). Use COP examples and evaluate the perspective.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "common but differentiated responsibilities (CBDR)".
items.answer: The principle that all states share responsibility for climate change but developed countries bear greater responsibility because of historical emissions and capacity
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the principle that all states share responsibility for climate change but developed countries bear greater responsibility because of historical emissions and capacity. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A student claims that developing countries have no obligations under international climate agreements. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Under the Paris Agreement all parties, including developing countries, submit NDCs; CBDR means differentiated, not zero, responsibilities.
items.markingKey: Under the Paris Agreement all parties, including developing countries, submit NDCs; CBDR means differentiated, not zero, responsibilities. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain how the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities might apply to negotiations between the EU and India.
items.answer: The EU has higher historical emissions and capacity, so it should cut faster and provide finance and technology; India has lower per-capita emissions and development needs but still contributes through its NDC (e.g. net zero by 2070).
items.markingKey: The EU has higher historical emissions and capacity, so it should cut faster and provide finance and technology; India has lower per-capita emissions and development needs but still contributes through its NDC (e.g. net zero by 2070).

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"We are not drowning. We are fighting."
— Slogan of the Pacific Climate Warriors network

With reference to the source, explain how Pacific Island states and activists have framed climate change.
items.answer: They reject being portrayed as passive victims and frame themselves as active agents demanding climate justice through activism, diplomacy and law (e.g. the ICJ advisory opinion).
items.markingKey: They reject being portrayed as passive victims and frame themselves as active agents demanding climate justice through activism, diplomacy and law (e.g. the ICJ advisory opinion). Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: "Climate justice requires developed countries to pay for loss and damage in developing countries." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: There is a strong justice case based on historical responsibility, but disputes over who pays and how much limit implementation.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: historical emissions; polluter pays principle; COP27 fund. Arguments against: China and Gulf states now major emitters; liability concerns; aid fatigue. Supported judgement: There is a strong justice case based on historical responsibility, but disputes over who pays and how much limit implementation. items.stem: What is an example of absolute decoupling?
items.answer: A country's GDP rising while its total carbon emissions fall
items.markingKey: A country's GDP rising while its total carbon emissions fall. The UK and Sweden have achieved absolute decoupling of territorial emissions.

items.stem: Explain why critics argue that green growth is not happening fast enough.
items.answer: Absolute decoupling has occurred only in some rich countries and at rates far too slow to meet 1.5°C; consumption-based emissions and material use are often outsourced to other countries.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Absolute decoupling has occurred only in some rich countries and at rates far too slow to meet 1.5°C; consumption-based emissions and material use are often outsourced to other countries. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between degrowth and green growth.
items.answer: Degrowth calls for planned reduction of production and consumption in rich countries to stay within ecological limits; green growth argues that growth can continue if decoupled from emissions through technology and markets.
items.markingKey: Degrowth calls for planned reduction of production and consumption in rich countries to stay within ecological limits; green growth argues that growth can continue if decoupled from emissions through technology and markets. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Lars writes: "The Global North–South divide is purely geographical." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It is a socio-economic and political category: Australia and New Zealand are in the "North", and the category hides large differences within both groups, such as between China and Malawi.
items.markingKey: It is a socio-economic and political category: Australia and New Zealand are in the "North", and the category hides large differences within both groups, such as between China and Malawi. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Solar power is now the cheapest electricity in history. The question is not whether we can grow and decarbonise, but how fast."
— Clean energy industry report, 2023 (adapted)

Identify the perspective in the source and explain one argument supporting it.
items.answer: Green growth: falling renewable costs make decarbonisation compatible with growth; clean industries create jobs and exports.
items.markingKey: Green growth: falling renewable costs make decarbonisation compatible with growth; clean industries create jobs and exports. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Discuss whether sustainable development is compatible with continued economic growth, using examples.
items.answer: Evaluate green growth (decoupling data, China's clean industry), degrowth (Hickel, Raworth), North–South equity (CBDR, JETPs); reach a reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: Evaluate green growth (decoupling data, China's clean industry), degrowth (Hickel, Raworth), North–South equity (CBDR, JETPs); reach a reasoned conclusion.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The argument that rich economies should deliberately reduce production and consumption to live within ecological limits while improving well-being"?
items.answer: degrowth
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of degrowth.

items.stem: Distinguish between territorial emissions and consumption-based emissions.
items.answer: Territorial emissions are produced within a country's borders; consumption-based emissions count emissions caused by the goods and services a country consumes, including imports produced elsewhere.
items.markingKey: Territorial emissions are produced within a country's borders; consumption-based emissions count emissions caused by the goods and services a country consumes, including imports produced elsewhere. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Chloé writes: "Degrowth means a recession." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Degrowth advocates distinguish planned, equitable reduction of material throughput with social protection from an unplanned recession that causes unemployment and hardship.
items.markingKey: Degrowth advocates distinguish planned, equitable reduction of material throughput with social protection from an unplanned recession that causes unemployment and hardship. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Identify which perspective each statement reflects: (a) "We need electric vehicles and carbon prices, not less prosperity", (b) "Rich countries must reduce material consumption", (c) "Our people need electricity first; the North must cut first."
items.answer: (a) green growth; (b) degrowth; (c) Global South/climate justice (CBDR) perspective. 1 mark each.
items.markingKey: (a) green growth; (b) degrowth; (c) Global South/climate justice (CBDR) perspective. 1 mark each.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "intergenerational equity".
items.answer: Fairness between present and future generations in the use of resources and the environment
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: fairness between present and future generations in the use of resources and the environment. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, adopted at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit, which provides the framework for climate negotiations"?
items.answer: UNFCCC
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of UNFCCC.

items.stem: What economists developed "doughnut economics"?
items.answer: Kate Raworth
items.markingKey: Kate Raworth. Doughnut Economics was published in 2017.

items.stem: Distinguish between the MDGs and the SDGs.
items.answer: The MDGs (2000–2015) had 8 goals focused on poverty and social development in developing countries; the SDGs (2015–2030) have 17 universal goals integrating economic, social and environmental dimensions.
items.markingKey: The MDGs (2000–2015) had 8 goals focused on poverty and social development in developing countries; the SDGs (2015–2030) have 17 universal goals integrating economic, social and environmental dimensions. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the Paris Agreement achieved wider participation than the Kyoto Protocol.
items.answer: Kyoto imposed binding targets only on developed countries, so the US refused and major emerging emitters had no obligations; Paris lets every country set its own NDC, so all major emitters, including China and India, joined.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Kyoto imposed binding targets only on developed countries, so the US refused and major emerging emitters had no obligations; Paris lets every country set its own NDC, so all major emitters, including China and India, joined. items.stem: Briefly explain why many Global South governments oppose degrowth.
items.answer: They argue that their citizens still need growth to escape poverty and build infrastructure; rich countries industrialised using fossil fuels, so asking poorer countries to limit growth is unjust – though degrowth advocates aim it at rich countries.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They argue that their citizens still need growth to escape poverty and build infrastructure; rich countries industrialised using fossil fuels, so asking poorer countries to limit growth is unjust – though degrowth advocates aim it at rich countries. items.stem: Briefly describe COP26 and the coal "phase-down" and explain what it reveals about national interests in climate negotiations.
items.answer: At COP26 in Glasgow (2021), India and China secured last-minute changes from "phase-out" to "phase-down" of unabated coal power. developing economies dependent on coal resisted stronger commitments, citing development needs and CBDR
items.markingKey: Context (At COP26 in Glasgow (2021), India and China secured last-minute changes from "phase-out" to "phase-down" of unabated coal power.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Country X's GDP grew by 30% between 2005 and 2023 while its territorial emissions fell by 25%, but its consumption-based emissions fell by only 5%. Explain what this suggests about decoupling.
items.answer: Absolute decoupling of territorial emissions, but much of the reduction may reflect outsourcing emissions-intensive production abroad; consumption-based decoupling is far weaker, so green growth claims are partly overstated.
items.markingKey: Absolute decoupling of territorial emissions, but much of the reduction may reflect outsourcing emissions-intensive production abroad; consumption-based decoupling is far weaker, so green growth claims are partly overstated.

items.stem: Mohammed writes: "The Paris Agreement legally requires every country to meet its emission-reduction targets." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Parties must prepare, communicate and update NDCs and report on progress, but achieving the targets is not legally binding and there are no sanctions.
items.markingKey: Parties must prepare, communicate and update NDCs and report on progress, but achieving the targets is not legally binding and there are no sanctions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"High-income nations are responsible for the vast majority of excess resource use. It is they who need to scale down, so that poorer nations can meet human needs."
— Paraphrase of Jason Hickel, Less Is More, 2020

With reference to the source, explain the degrowth argument and why it targets rich countries.
items.answer: Degrowth holds that rich countries exceed fair shares of resources and should reduce material throughput, creating ecological space for poorer countries to develop.
items.markingKey: Degrowth holds that rich countries exceed fair shares of resources and should reduce material throughput, creating ecological space for poorer countries to develop. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: A government plans a coal mine that will create 5,000 jobs. Using the three pillars of sustainability, outline the trade-offs.
items.answer: Economic: jobs, revenue, energy security; social: local employment but health impacts and displacement; environmental: emissions, pollution, biodiversity loss. Judgement on balance. 1 per pillar + 1 judgement.
items.markingKey: Economic: jobs, revenue, energy security; social: local employment but health impacts and displacement; environmental: emissions, pollution, biodiversity loss. Judgement on balance. 1 per pillar + 1 judgement.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"We did not cause this crisis, yet we are asked to pay for it with our farms, our homes and our children's future."
— Statement by a negotiator for the Least Developed Countries group, 2022 (adapted)

Explain, with reference to the source, the concept of climate justice.
items.answer: Those least responsible for emissions bear the greatest costs, so justice requires major emitters to cut emissions and finance adaptation and loss and damage.

items.stem: Distinguish between weak sustainability and strong sustainability.
items.answer: Weak sustainability allows natural capital to be replaced by human-made capital as long as total capital is maintained; strong sustainability holds that critical natural capital (e.g. climate stability, biodiversity) cannot be substituted.
items.markingKey: Weak sustainability allows natural capital to be replaced by human-made capital as long as total capital is maintained; strong sustainability holds that critical natural capital (e.g. climate stability, biodiversity) cannot be substituted. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why climate change raises issues of justice.
items.answer: Rich industrialised countries are responsible for most historical emissions, while poorer countries and small island states (e.g. Tuvalu, Bangladesh) suffer most from sea-level rise, droughts and storms and have least capacity to adapt.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Rich industrialised countries are responsible for most historical emissions, while poorer countries and small island states (e.g. Tuvalu, Bangladesh) suffer most from sea-level rise, droughts and storms and have least capacity to adapt. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims that the Global North–South divide is purely geographical. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It is a socio-economic and political category: Australia and New Zealand are in the "North", and the category hides large differences within both groups, such as between China and Malawi.
items.markingKey: It is a socio-economic and political category: Australia and New Zealand are in the "North", and the category hides large differences within both groups, such as between China and Malawi. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between mitigation and adaptation.
items.answer: Mitigation means reducing greenhouse gas emissions or increasing carbon sinks to limit climate change; adaptation means adjusting to its effects, such as building sea walls or drought-resistant crops.
items.markingKey: Mitigation means reducing greenhouse gas emissions or increasing carbon sinks to limit climate change; adaptation means adjusting to its effects, such as building sea walls or drought-resistant crops. items.stem: Explain why supporters believe green growth is possible.
items.answer: Renewable energy costs have fallen dramatically, and several countries have cut emissions while growing; technology, carbon pricing and investment (e.g. the EU Green Deal, US Inflation Reduction Act) can drive growth in clean industries.

items.stem: With reference to Costa Rica's reforestation, explain how it illustrates sustainable development in practice.
items.answer: Costa Rica reversed deforestation through payments for ecosystem services from 1997; forest cover rose from about a fifth to over half of its territory. policy aligned economic incentives with environmental goals, combining conservation and development
items.markingKey: Context (Costa Rica reversed deforestation through payments for ecosystem services from 1997; forest cover rose from about a fifth to over half of its territory.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: policy aligned economic incentives with environmental goals, combining conservation and development – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to sustainable development in practice.

items.stem: "The Paris Agreement legally requires every country to meet its emission-reduction targets." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Parties must prepare, communicate and update NDCs and report on progress, but achieving the targets is not legally binding and there are no sanctions.
items.markingKey: Parties must prepare, communicate and update NDCs and report on progress, but achieving the targets is not legally binding and there are no sanctions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that degrowth means a recession. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Degrowth advocates distinguish planned, equitable reduction of material throughput with social protection from an unplanned recession that causes unemployment and hardship.
items.markingKey: Degrowth advocates distinguish planned, equitable reduction of material throughput with social protection from an unplanned recession that causes unemployment and hardship. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using Tuvalu and sea-level rise as an example, explain climate justice and sovereignty.
items.answer: Tuvalu, a low-lying Pacific state, faces existential threats from rising seas; in 2023 it signed the Falepili Union with Australia allowing some citizens to migrate and recognising its statehood regardless of territorial loss. a state that contributed little to emissions faces the possible loss of territory, raising new questions about statehood and responsibility

items.stem: With reference to China's green industrial strategy, explain how it illustrates green growth.
items.answer: China leads the world in production of solar panels, wind turbines, batteries and electric vehicles, while still building new coal plants. clean technology is a major source of growth and exports, though high coal use shows the limits of decoupling

items.answer: Rwanda banned non-biodegradable plastic bags in 2008 and is often cited as one of the cleanest countries in Africa. strong state enforcement delivered environmental goals, though critics note limited political freedoms

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that the Paris Agreement has been a success.
items.answer: Paris succeeded in creating a universal framework, but has not yet delivered emission cuts consistent with its goals.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: near-universal participation; ratchet mechanism; NDC targets have lowered projected warming from ~4°C. Arguments against: current path ~2.5–3°C; not enforceable; US withdrawals; finance shortfalls. Supported judgement: Paris succeeded in creating a universal framework, but has not yet delivered emission cuts consistent with its goals.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that green growth is a more realistic path to sustainability than degrowth?
items.answer: Green growth is more politically realistic, but without reduced consumption in rich countries it may not be fast enough.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: falling renewable costs; politically acceptable; decoupling in UK, Sweden. Arguments against: decoupling too slow; material use still rising; rebound effects; degrowth addresses consumption. Supported judgement: Green growth is more politically realistic, but without reduced consumption in rich countries it may not be fast enough. items.stem: To what extent is it true that the Sustainable Development Goals are too ambitious to be achieved?
items.answer: Most SDGs will not be met by 2030, but their value lies in shaping priorities and accountability rather than full achievement.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: 17 goals and 169 targets; only a small share on track; financing gap of trillions. Arguments against: goals set direction and mobilise action; MDGs saw real progress; universal framework.
